title: Ἔριφος ⟨ἐπὶ δώματος ἑστὼς⟩ καὶ λύκος
titleEn: The Kid on the Roof and the Wolf
part: The Kid on the Roof and the Wolf (Chambry 106 · Perry 98)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 106 (= Perry 98). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔριφος ἐπί τινος δώματος ἑστώς, ἐπειδὴ λύκον παριόντα εἶδεν, ἐλοιδόρει καὶ ἔσκωπτεν αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Eriphos epi tinos dōmatos hestōs, epeidē lykon parionta eiden, eloidorei kai eskōpten auton.
sentences.l: A kid, standing on a certain housetop, when he saw a wolf passing by, kept reviling and mocking him.
sentences.n: ἑστώς is the perfect participle of ἵστημι used intransitively: the perfect of this verb is not past but present in force — one who has taken his stand simply stands. δῶμα is the house, and ἐπὶ δώματος puts the kid on its flat roof, which is the whole point: he is out of reach. ἐλοιδόρει and ἔσκωπτεν are imperfects — he kept at it.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λύκος ἔφη· « Ὦ οὗτος, οὐ σύ με λοιδορεῖς, ἀλλ’ ὁ τόπος. »
sentences.tr: Ho de lykos ephē· « Ō houtos, ou sy me loidoreis, all’ ho topos. »
sentences.l: And the wolf said: « You there, it is not you that revile me, but the place. »
sentences.n: Ὦ οὗτος is the ordinary Greek hail across a distance — 'you there!' — brusque rather than courteous. The negative attaches to the pronoun and not to the verb: not you but the place is doing the reviling.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πολλάκις καὶ ὁ τόπος καὶ ὁ καιρὸς δίδωσι τὸ θράσος κατὰ τῶν ἀμεινόνων.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti pollakis kai ho topos kai ho kairos didōsi to thrasos kata tōn ameinonōn.
sentences.l: The fable shows that often both the place and the occasion give boldness against one's betters.
sentences.n: καὶ … καί couples the two: not one or the other but both together. θράσος is nerve, effrontery — the bad kind of boldness, set against θάρσος, which is courage. οἱ ἀμείνονες is the comparative of ἀγαθός used as a noun, 'the better men', those one stands below. δίδωσι is singular although two subjects stand before it; Greek often keeps the singular with two singular subjects joined by καί.
